verdict:
This is a novel about the partial record: about how five words can be technically accurate and functionally a lie, about how the certified transcript and the excerpt are not the same document. Ellen Vance, a court reporter in a small West Virginia town, buys a house in which a woman died of hypothermia in February 1983, and the book's form — documentary, archival, building toward what the files cannot contain — mirrors her professional discipline. The result is one of the more rigorous formal achievements I have encountered in recent fiction: a novel in which what the narrator does for work is also what the novel does as work, without once making this explicit. The court reporter's ethics become the novel's moral argument, delivered through structure rather than statement.

The dual-timeline architecture alternates between Ellen's present-day investigation and the first-person voice of Della Markey during her last night. This hauntological arrangement is the novel's most original contribution: Della, narrating from some post-death version of the house's continuous present, senses Ellen as warmth at the wrong angle — weather from another season bleeding through the back-room door. Ellen registers Della as cold without mechanical explanation, a door that will not stay latched. Neither woman knows what she is registering; no explanation is offered. The novel works this mutual-invisible-presence device with striking control across every chapter it enters, never overclaiming and never undercutting. The revelation that "Nobody came to that door" is five precise words at the end of a twenty-nine-word paragraph that documents the knocking, the recognition, and the refusal — that the county never had the paragraph, only the sentence — is earned by patient accumulation across the full length of the book. This is how revelations should arrive.

But the book contains production artifacts that self-sabotage its central claim. A novel whose argument rests on documentary precision cannot afford to place Della's tin of matches in four different locations across the Della chapters — shelf above the stove in chapter 2, coat pocket in chapter 6, drawer to the left of the sink in chapter 12, kitchen shelf in chapter 14 — without explanation. More seriously, the inquest witness statement in chapter 11 places Mabel Duff's last sighting of Della "on the evening of February tenth," but the February 10 ledger entry in chapter 21 records the same encounter "in the morning, before conditions worsened." Chapter 23 renders the property address as "14 Verrill Street." These contradictions exist in a book that builds its moral architecture on the difference between "an excerpt" and "a certified record." They are correctable before publication. Before correction, they are not small in a novel that has defined its own standard as the certified transcript.

The middle section — four courthouse visits across roughly seven chapters — tests a reader's patience in the way the courthouse tests patience: correctly but repetitively. The prose quality sustains this section but barely, and it is the most likely place to lose a reader who has not yet committed to the book's pace. What prevents the repetition from being fatal is the accumulating documentary weight and the alternating Della chapters, which grow more harrowing as the temperature falls. The ending earns what few endings do: not resolution, not comfort, but the right and permanent condition of the house. When Ellen carries Della's travel clock downstairs in the final chapter, she does not understand this as a gesture toward the dead. It is simply the correct arrangement of objects. The novel knows what it is doing, and that is rare.

strongest.claim: Sentence-level prose in both voices achieves documentary plainness (Ellen) and ledger-column spareness (Della) without slipping into monotony or sentimentality. The opening description of the back room — 'the cold of a room that had been cold for a long time and had organized itself around that fact, the way rooms organize themselves around their particular silences' — does what a competent-but-ordinary line does not: it grants the room an interiority and makes it a subject, not a setting.

The central formal device — the phrase 'Nobody came to that door' accumulating weight and then being dismantled against its containing paragraph — is constructed with genuine structural patience. The revelation in chapters 21 and 22 that the five words are the close of a twenty-nine-word entry that documents the knocking, the recognition, and the refusal is fully earned by the preceding twenty chapters of evidence. The court reporter's professional ethics (an excerpt is not a guarantee) become the novel's moral instrument without ever being announced as such.

The hauntological mutual perception — Della sensing Ellen as 'warmth at the wrong angle,' Ellen sensing Della as cold without mechanical explanation — is handled with uncommon formal discipline. The novel never specifies the ontology; it finds a third option between 'the ghost speaks' and 'there is no ghost,' and holds it. The device is introduced in chapter 8 and elaborated in chapter 10 without ever being overclaimed in the chapters that follow.

The object network — the Renick Furniture Works desk, the travel clock, the staircase's third step, the oil lamp, the account book — migrates across both timelines without authorial underlining. These are not symbols; they are objects with documented histories that accrue meaning through their presence in two lives. The final chapter's action of carrying the travel clock downstairs completes a circuit without naming it.

The ending earns what it claims. 'And Della —' stopping mid-sentence before 'The house was quiet. / The door was open.' is the only moment in Ellen's chapters where Della is named without bureaucratic mediation, and the sentence is stopped. The interruption is the right formal gesture for a woman who cannot be completed, in a novel that has insisted throughout that the record must be complete. The back-room door, open, is resolution without resolution being named.

weakest.claim: The matches change location four times across the Della chapters without explanation: on the shelf above the stove in chapter 2 (twelve of them); in her coat pocket after the second fire attempt in chapter 6 ('I put the tin back in my coat pocket'); in the drawer to the left of the sink in chapter 12 ('the two matches are in the tin in the drawer to the left of the sink, where they have always been kept in this house'); and on the kitchen shelf in chapter 14. In a book that explicitly valorizes exact inventory ('two matches, not a handful'), this is a continuity failure that undermines the novel's central claim to documentary precision.

The inquest witness statement in chapter 11 places Mabel Duff's last sighting of Della 'on the evening of February tenth,' while the February 10 ledger entry in chapter 21 records the same encounter 'in the morning, before conditions worsened.' Chapter 23 (from the revision draft) repeats the 'evening' version. The novel cannot hold both simultaneously. This is either a production error or a deliberate discrepancy the novel never acknowledges — and in a book built around the careful reading of witness testimony, an unacknowledged discrepancy between two source documents is a structural problem.

Chapter 23 contains a production artifact: the property address is rendered as 'to the residence at 14 Verrill Street' where the address is 412 Verrill Street, stated consistently throughout the novel. This is a typo — '412' collapsed to '14' — of the kind that proofreading catches. In any other novel it would be a minor annoyance. In a novel that cites property addresses from deed records as evidence, it reads as careless.

The research section — four courthouse visits across chapters 7 through 15, each structured around Ellen reading a new document in the records room — is repetitive in procedure without sufficient formal variation between visits. The prose quality is sustained throughout, but the structural similarity of the scenes (drive to Lewisburg, sign in at the counter, read in order, photograph, drive back) creates a monotony that risks losing a reader who has not yet committed to the novel's pace. The novel would benefit from compressing at least one of these visits.

Ellen's professional identity is rendered with great precision, but her inner life remains largely withheld. 'Martinsburg' hangs in the background — work that 'had not come back up, not to what they had been' — without content. By the final chapter we have inhabited Della's inner life fully: her father, her brother, her choice at the door. We have never quite entered Ellen's. The asymmetry is partly intentional — Ellen's emotional work is conducted through professional displacement — but it tips toward Ellen functioning as a vehicle for the reader rather than a second subject of the novel.

quotes.text: Spring light, thin and without opinion, moved on the south-facing windows.
quotes.why: The light is given a moral quality — 'without opinion' — that prefigures the novel's entire formal stance: to describe without editorializing, to receive the record without interpretation. It also does it in ten words.

quotes.text: the cold of a room that had been cold for a long time and had organized itself around that fact, the way rooms organize themselves around their particular silences
quotes.why: The room 'organizing itself' around cold grants the back room interiority without supernatural assertion. A competent-but-ordinary line would say the room 'felt cold' or describe insulation failures. This line makes the room a subject, which is what the novel needs it to be.

quotes.text: Three years I have not written his name but I knew it.
quotes.why: The sentence performs the novel's central argument at the level of the sentence: what is not in the record does not stop being known. 'I knew it' is present tense in a past-tense entry, which is the right grammar for something that hasn't stopped being true.

quotes.text: An excerpt was not a guarantee.
quotes.why: The moral claim of the entire novel in five words, delivered as professional procedure rather than ethical assertion. The novel earns the right to say it here because it has spent twenty chapters demonstrating it.

quotes.text: the record goes into the material and stays
quotes.why: The thematic culmination placed at the level of the desk's maker's mark — not abstracted into theme but grounded in a specific object that has been present since chapter 1. The permanence of the inscription and the permanence of Della's ledger entry are made the same kind of fact.

put_down_points: Chapters 11, 13, and 15 — three consecutive courthouse-visit chapters with near-identical procedural structures (drive to Lewisburg, sign in at the counter, read in order, photograph pages, drive north). A reader who has not committed to the novel's pace will lose patience here. The individual prose is sustained; the structural repetition is not justified by sufficient formal variation between visits.
who_is_this_for: Readers of Marilynne Robinson's Gilead, Denis Johnson's earlier short fiction, and Sarah Moss's Ghost Wall — readers who can give a quiet novel the attention it requires and who find formal architecture as satisfying as plot mechanics. Not for readers who want forward momentum, genre satisfactions, or emotional directness. This is a novel in which the form is the argument, which is either the most interesting thing about it or an obstacle, depending entirely on the reader.
